newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Britain's last troops in Hong Kong mix pomp, sweat.
newsitem.headline: Britain's last troops in Hong Kong mix pomp, sweat.

text.p: Like the kilts and camouflage in their kitbags, Scotland's Black Watch mix ceremony and hard slogging as they prepare to pipe Britain out of Hong Kong in June and close up shop as the last colonial troops.

"We now have the privilege to be the last regiment in Hong Kong," commanding officer Lieutenant-Colonel Alistair Louden told reporters on Monday at the regiment's base on Stonecutters Island, in the heart of the territory's docklands.

The Black Watch -- dubbed the "Highland Furies" by the French after the Battle of Fontenoy in 1745 and wrapped in a blue and green tartan so dark it is nearly black -- began its historic 138-day assignment last Thursday when it replaced the Staffordshire Regiment.
For most of the regiment, the new posting is a familiar one. The Black Watch was the resident infantry battalion of the Hong Kong Garrison from January 1993 until August 1994.
"It's good to be back -- nice to see the place again," said Pipe Major Steven Small, who splits his time between cradling a machinegun and the bagpipes.
"In a time like now, there's quite a bit of high-profile stuff we'll be asked to do, so we're likely to be busy on both fronts."

Since the end of World War Two, the Black Watch has served in Korea, Kenya and Cyprus and has conducted 11 tours of Northern Ireland. Their motto is "nemo me impune lacessit" -- "nobody provokes me without being hurt".

For their first 12 weeks in Hong Kong, the 551 soldiers will rotate through a mix of duties, from guarding important installations and helping Hong Kong police combat smugglers to training in the rugged, green hills of the New Territories.

By May 1, two-fifths of the regiment will have returned to base at Fort George near Inverness, Scotland. The rest will close down the army's facilities, which will be handed over to China along with the rest of the British colony at midnight on June 30, and drill for the ceremonies surrounding the handover.
"I think it's going to involve a lot of nose to the grindstone work," said Captain Alasdair Halford-MacLeod.

The regiment will parade through the streets of Hong Kong in their dark kilts and plumed bonnets and on June 30 will stand alongside colonial Governor Chris Patten and Chinese officials at the ceremony marking the historic change of sovereignty.
